claim: TRIM5α is a restriction factor that intercepts the incoming capsids of diverse retroviruses, including HIV-1, and inhibits viral replication.
source: TRIM5α is a restriction factor that intercepts the incoming capsids of diverse retroviruses, including HIV-1, and inhibits viral replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Sayah et al., 2004; Stremlau et al., 2004; 2006) that established TRIM5α's role as a restriction factor.

claim: The mechanism of TRIM5α restriction is primarily associated with premature termination of reverse transcription and accelerated dissociation of the viral core.
source: The mechanism of restriction is not yet fully understood, but is primarily associated with premature termination of reverse transcription and accelerated dissociation of the viral core (Sayah et al., 2004; Stremlau et al., 2004; 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Sayah et al., 2004; Stremlau et al., 2004; 2006).

claim: TRIM5α is proposed to be a pattern recognition receptor for retroviral capsids that initiates a signaling cascade to induce type I interferon upon capsid binding.
source: TRIM5α is also proposed to be a pattern recognition receptor for retroviral capsids, in that it initiates a signaling cascade to induce type I interferon upon capsid binding (Pertel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pertel et al., 2011.

claim: Ubiquitin is implicated in both the antiviral (restriction) and signaling activities of TRIM5α.
source: Ubiquitin (Ub) is implicated in both the antiviral (restriction) and signaling activities of TRIM5α.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent discussion of TRIM5α's E3 ligase activity and ubiquitination functions.

claim: TRIM5α's E3 ligase activity creates K63-linked polyUb chains.
source: In particular, TRIM5α's E3 ligase activity creates K63-linked polyUb chains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of the manuscript discussing TRIM5α's enzymatic activity.

claim: TRIM5α self-ligation correlates with the block in reverse transcription.
source: TRIM5α self-ligation correlates with the block in reverse transcription (Campbell et al., 2015; Fletcher et al., 2015; Roa et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2015; Fletcher et al., 2015; Roa et al., 2012.

claim: Unanchored polyubiquitin chains have been proposed to mediate interferon signaling by TRIM5α.
source: whereas unanchored chains have been proposed to mediate interferon signaling (Pertel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pertel et al., 2011.

claim: TRIM5α consists of an N-terminal tripartite or RBCC motif (RING, B-box 2, and coiled-coil domains), followed by a C-terminal domain.
source: Like all TRIM proteins, TRIM5α consists of an N-terminal tripartite or RBCC motif (RING, B-box 2, and coiled-coil domains), followed by a C-terminal domain (Figure 1A) (Meroni and Diez-Roux, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Meroni and Diez-Roux, 2005 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The B-box 2 and coiled-coil domains make an integrated antiparallel dimer fold.
source: The B-box 2 and coiled-coil domains make an integrated antiparallel dimer fold (Goldstone et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldstone et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015.

claim: The B-box 2 and coiled-coil dimer acts as a scaffold that organizes the upstream and downstream domains.
source: which acts as a scaffold that organizes the upstream and downstream domains (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B and the structural context.

claim: In TRIM5α, the C-terminal domain is a β-sandwich fold called SPRY (or PRYSPRY/B30.2), which mediates direct binding to retroviral capsids.
source: In TRIM5α, the C-terminal domain is a β-sandwich fold called SPRY (or PRYSPRY/B30.2), which mediates direct binding to retroviral capsids (Biris et al., 2012; 2013; Diaz-Griffero et al., 2006b; Kovalskyy and Ivanov, 2014; Sawyer et al., 2005; Sayah et al., 2004; Sebastian and Luban, 2005; Stremlau et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Biris et al., 2012; 2013; Diaz-Griffero et al., 2006b; Kovalskyy and Ivanov, 2014; Sawyer et al., 2005; Sayah et al., 2004; Sebastian and Luban, 2005; Stremlau et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2012).

claim: The L2 linker that connects the SPRY domain to the coiled-coil packs against the coiled-coil scaffold.
source: The L2 linker that connects the SPRY domain to the coiled-coil packs against the coiled-coil scaffold
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies (Goldstone et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015).

claim: In the TRIM5α dimer, two SPRY domains are oriented to bind the capsid simultaneously.
source: and so in the TRIM5α dimer, two SPRY domains are oriented to bind the capsid simultaneously (Figure 1B) (Goldstone et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies (Goldstone et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Capsid recognition by TRIM5α is an avidity-driven interaction that only occurs in context of assembled capsid and assembled TRIM5α.
source: Capsid recognition by TRIM5α is an avidity-driven interaction; that is, productive binding only occurs in context of assembled capsid and assembled TRIM5α (Sebastian and Luban, 2005; Stremlau et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sebastian and Luban, 2005; Stremlau et al., 2006.

claim: Higher-order assembly of TRIM5α requires the B-box 2 domain.
source: Higher-order assembly of TRIM5α requires the B-box 2 domain
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009; Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Javanbakht et al., 2005; Li and Sodroski, 2008; Li et al., 2016).

claim: The B-box 2 domain mediates three-fold symmetric interactions that connect coiled-coil mediated TRIM5α dimers into a hexagonal net.
source: which is thought to mediate three-fold symmetric interactions that connect coiled-coil mediated TRIM5α dimers into a hexagonal net (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009; Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Javanbakht et al., 2005; Li and Sodroski, 2008; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009; Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Javanbakht et al., 2005; Li and Sodroski, 2008; Li et al., 2016).

claim: The hexagonal scaffold positions the SPRY domains to match the orientations of their corresponding binding epitopes on retroviral capsids.
source: This hexagonal scaffold is proposed to position the SPRY domains to match the orientations – both translational and rotational – of their corresponding binding epitopes on retroviral capsids
evidence: This claim is based on the proposed model of TRIM5α assembly and capsid recognition.

claim: The hexagonal scaffold generates powerful avidity effects that amplify very weak (millimolar level) intrinsic affinities between the SPRY and capsid subunits.
source: and thereby generate powerful avidity effects that amplify very weak (millimolar level (Biris et al., 2013)) intrinsic affinities between the SPRY and capsid subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biris et al., 2013 regarding the weak intrinsic affinity.

claim: The RBcc miniTRIM contained residues 1–159 from rhesus TRIM5α followed by an antiparallel coiled-coil hairpin derived from a bacterial seryl-tRNA synthetase and then residues 225–265 of the TRIM5α coiled-coil.
source: The 'RBcc' miniTRIM contained residues 1–159 from rhesus TRIM5α (which includes the RING, B-box 2, and the first 26 residues of the coiled-coil) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, colored in orange), followed by an antiparallel coiled-coil hairpin derived from a bacterial seryl-tRNA synthetase (residues 49–78 of PDB 1SRY, gray), and then residues 225–265 of the TRIM5α coiled-coil (green).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design of the miniTRIM construct.

claim: The Bcc miniTRIM lacks the RING domain (residues 1–88).
source: To further uncouple the B-box from potential dimeric interactions of the upstream RING domain, we also designed a second construct denoted 'Bcc' that lacks the RING (residues 1–88) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design of the Bcc miniTRIM construct.

claim: Both the RBcc and Bcc miniTRIMs proved well behaved in solution and could be purified to homogeneity.
source: Both the RBcc and Bcc miniTRIMs proved well behaved in solution, and could be purified to homogeneity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1E showing purification results.

claim: R121A and R121E mutants are deficient in capsid binding and restriction activities, correlating with defects in higher-order assembly.
source: Biochemical and cell-based assays show that R121A and R121E mutants are deficient in capsid binding and restriction activities, and this correlates with defects in higher-order assembly (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009; Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Li and Sodroski, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009; Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Li and Sodroski, 2008).

claim: The Arg121 surface patch mediates self-association of the isolated B-box 2 domain in solution.
source: The same patch also mediates self-association of the isolated B-box 2 domain in solution (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009.

claim: Both the RBcc miniTRIM and Bcc miniTRIM eluted early from a Superdex 75 size exclusion column as asymmetric peaks with sharp leading edges and pronounced tails.
source: Consistent with expectation, both the RBcc miniTRIM (Figure 1F) and Bcc miniTRIM (Figure 1G) eluted early from a Superdex 75 size exclusion column as asymmetric peaks with sharp leading edges and pronounced tails (blue traces).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: MiniTRIMs harboring the R121E mutation eluted late as more symmetrical peaks with elution volumes consistent with monomeric species.
source: In contrast, miniTRIMs harboring the R121E mutation eluted late as more symmetrical peaks (Figure 1F and G, red traces), with elution volumes consistent with monomeric species.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: The protein-protein interactions required for higher-order assembly of full-length TRIM5α are essential for miniTRIM oligomerization.
source: These results indicate that the protein-protein interactions required for higher-order assembly of full-length TRIM5α are also essential for miniTRIM oligomerization.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the size exclusion chromatography results.

claim: High quality synchrotron diffraction data were obtained from three crystal forms of Bcc miniTRIM.
source: We obtained high quality synchrotron diffraction data from three crystal forms of Bcc miniTRIM.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: A P212121 crystal contained two trimers in the asymmetric unit at 3.26 Å resolution with R/Rfree = 0.26/0.30.
source: A P212121 crystal contained two trimers in the asymmetric unit (3.26 Å resolution, R/Rfree = 0.26/0.30)
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: A C2 crystal form contained one dimer at 2.1 Å resolution with R/Rfree = 0.18/0.22.
source: a C2 form contained one dimer (2.1 Å, R/Rfree = 0.18/0.22)
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: A P1 crystal form contained two dimers at 2.3 Å resolution with R/Rfree = 0.22/0.26.
source: and a P1 form contained two dimers (2.3 Å, R/Rfree = 0.22/0.26) (Table 1 and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The three crystal forms yielded 12 crystallographically independent views of Bcc miniTRIM.
source: Altogether, these yielded 12 crystallographically independent views of Bcc miniTRIM.
evidence: This claim is based on the number of subunits in the asymmetric units of the three crystal forms.

claim: All 12 Bcc miniTRIM structures were very similar to each other.
source: All 12 structures were very similar to each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Electron densities for the B-box 2 domains and proximal regions of the coiled-coil domains were well defined.
source: In general, electron densities for the B-box 2 domains and proximal regions of the coiled-coil domains were well defined (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2B showing electron density maps.

claim: Densities for the hairpin linker were of poorer quality or missing in some cases.
source: whereas densities for the hairpin linker were of poorer quality or, in some cases, missing (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2C showing electron density maps.

claim: The 12 Bcc miniTRIM structures superimpose very well with the crystal structure of the TRIM5α B-box 2/coiled-coil dimer (PDB 4TN3).
source: Our 12 Bcc miniTRIM structures superimpose very well with the crystal structure of the TRIM5α B-box 2/coiled-coil dimer (PDB 4TN3) (Goldstone et al., 2014) (Figure 2D–F and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figures 2D-F and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The miniTRIM constructs are excellent structural surrogates for the B-box/coiled-coil core of the full RBCC motif.
source: This indicates that our miniTRIM constructs are excellent structural surrogates for the B-box/coiled-coil core of the full RBCC motif.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structural similarity between miniTRIM and full-length TRIM5α structures.

claim: The Bcc miniTRIM trimer is organized as a triskelion with three B-box 2 domains making a central three-fold symmetric vertex from which the coiled-coil domains emanate as spokes.
source: The Bcc miniTRIM trimer is organized as a triskelion: three B-box 2 domains make a central three-fold symmetric vertex from which the coiled-coil domains emanate as spokes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The trimerization interactions are principally mediated by the B-box domain, burying 578 Å2 of the available surface area from each subunit.
source: As expected, the trimerization interactions are principally mediated by the B-box domain, burying 578 Å2 of the available surface area from each subunit.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the trimer interface.

claim: The three-fold vertexes of the TRIM5α hexagonal lattice are made by B-box trimers.
source: This result indicates that the three-fold vertexes of the TRIM5α hexagonal lattice are made by B-box trimers.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the trimer structure and its implications for lattice assembly.

claim: The B-box packs against the N-terminal end of the coiled-coil helix through a hydrophobic interface.
source: The B-box packs against the N-terminal end of the coiled-coil helix through a hydrophobic interface (Figure 3A, asterisks)
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Trimer formation requires the presence of the coiled-coil.
source: suggesting that trimer formation requires the presence of the coiled-coil.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed B-box/coiled-coil packing interactions.

claim: Higher-order assembly into a hexagonal lattice is a function of the integrated tripartite motif of TRIM5α and does not simply arise from combining otherwise independent self-association motifs.
source: This observation is consistent with the idea that higher-order assembly into a hexagonal lattice is a function of the integrated tripartite motif of TRIM5α, and does not simply arise from combining otherwise independent self-association motifs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structural observations of B-box/coiled-coil interactions.

claim: The majority of Bcc miniTRIM crystals obtained were composed of dimers.
source: Interestingly, the majority of Bcc miniTRIM crystals we obtained (including three other forms that we did not refine) were composed of dimers (Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on crystallographic observations.

claim: The dimer is quasi-equivalent to the trimer with the same sets of residues making the same interactions but with valence of two instead of three.
source: The dimer is quasi-equivalent to the trimer: the same sets of residues make the same interactions but with valence of two instead of three.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison of the dimer and trimer interfaces.

claim: The dimer buries a smaller surface area per subunit (450 Å2) compared to the trimer (578 Å2).
source: The dimer buries a smaller surface area per subunit (450 Å2) compared to the trimer.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the interfaces.

claim: Both the trimer and dimer are stabilized by three layers of interactions, with a hydrophobic layer sandwiched between two hydrophilic layers.
source: Both the trimer and dimer are stabilized by three layers of interactions, with a hydrophobic layer sandwiched between two hydrophilic layers (Figure 3B,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structures shown in Figures 3B and 3H.

claim: The top layers make a ring of salt bridges mediated by Glu102 and Lys103 from each subunit.
source: The top layers (closest to the N-termini of the B-boxes) make a ring of salt bridges mediated by Glu102 and Lys103 from each subunit (Figure 3D,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structures shown in Figures 3D and 3J.

claim: The middle, hydrophobic layers center on Trp117.
source: The middle, hydrophobic layers center on Trp117 (Figure 3E,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structures shown in Figures 3E and 3K.

claim: In both oligomers, the Trp117 indole sidechains make a hydrophobic core surrounded by a collar of close packed leucine sidechains (Leu105, Leu106, Leu118, and Leu132).
source: In both oligomers, these indole sidechains make a hydrophobic core surrounded by a collar of close packed leucine sidechains (Leu105, Leu106, Leu118, and Leu132).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the hydrophobic layer.

claim: The third, bottom layers consist of a ring of salt bridges with Glu120 and Arg121.
source: The third, bottom layers also consist of a ring of salt bridges, this time with Glu120 and Arg121 (Figure 3F,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structures shown in Figures 3F and 3L.

claim: At the periphery of the bottom layer, the sidechain hydroxyl of Thr30 donates a hydrogen bond to Glu120.
source: At the periphery of this layer, the sidechain hydroxyl of Thr30 donates a hydrogen bond to Glu120.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the bottom layer interactions.

claim: Interactions between the layers consist of a hydrogen bond between Glu102 (top) and the indole amide of Trp117 (middle), and close packing between the Trp117 sidechain (middle) and the Arg121 sidechain guanidinium group (bottom).
source: Interactions between the layers consist of a hydrogen bond between Glu102 (top) and the indole amide of Trp117 (middle), and close packing between the Trp117 sidechain (middle) and the Arg121 sidechain guanidinium group (bottom) (Figure 3C,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structures shown in Figures 3C and 3I.

claim: The Trp117 indoles in the trimer form a channel that would be expected to have a highly negatively charged hole at the center.
source: The Trp117 indoles in the trimer form a channel that would be expected to have a highly negatively charged hole at the center (Figure 3E)
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis and inference about electrostatic properties.

claim: The negatively charged hole at the center of the Trp117 channel is likely to be partially stabilized by the positively charged Arg121 sidechains.
source: which is likely to be partially stabilized by the positively charged Arg121 sidechains.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on electrostatic considerations.

claim: The trimer and dimer are distinguished primarily by intermolecular packing between the Trp117, Leu118, and Leu132 sidechains in the hydrophobic layer.
source: Comparison of the trimer and dimer bonding interactions revealed that the two oligomers are distinguished primarily by intermolecular packing between the Trp117, Leu118, and Leu132 sidechains in the hydrophobic layer.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison of the trimer and dimer.

claim: Leu118 and Leu132 are in van der Waals contact in the trimer, but more separated in the dimer.
source: In particular, Leu118 and Leu132, which are located at the outer edges of the binding surface, are in van der Waals contact in the trimer, but more separated in the dimer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first two turns of the coiled-coil helix are overwound and bent in the dimer form.
source: Another distinction is that the first two turns of the coiled-coil helix are overwound and bent in the dimer form (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The bending of the coiled-coil helix in the dimer might indicate some structural communication between the interacting B-boxes and the coiled-coil domain.
source: which might indicate some structural communication between the interacting B-boxes and the coiled-coil domain.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the observed structural differences.

claim: Both the W117E and R121E Bcc miniTRIM mutants were monomeric in AUC experiments.
source: In control experiments, both the W117E and R121E Bcc miniTRIM mutants were monomeric, in agreement with the structures (not shown)
evidence: This claim is based on AUC experimental data.

claim: The wildtype Bcc miniTRIM distributions indicated self-association in AUC experiments.
source: whereas the wildtype (WT) Bcc distributions indicated self-association (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by AUC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Global fitting of the WT Bcc miniTRIM equilibrium distributions to a monomer-dimer-trimer model only returned stable values for the monomer-dimer dissociation constant (1 μM).
source: Global fitting of the WT equilibrium distributions to a monomer-dimer-trimer model only returned stable values for the monomer-dimer dissociation constant (1 μM).
evidence: This claim is based on AUC data analysis.

claim: The AUC data gave a satisfactory fit to a monomer-dimer equilibrium model, indicating that trimers (or higher-order oligomers than dimers) were disfavored in solution.
source: Indeed, the AUC data gave a satisfactory fit to a monomer-dimer equilibrium model, indicating that trimers (or higher-order oligomers than dimers) were disfavored in solution.
evidence: This claim is based on AUC data analysis.

claim: SEC-MALS analysis at 0.9 mM showed that the Bcc miniTRIM was predominantly dimeric in solution with some higher-order species present at a much smaller fraction.
source: The mass trace (blue curve in Figure 3—figure supplement 4) had a sharp peak at the leading edge of the protein absorbance peak (black curve), a curved plateau in the central region above the expected mass for a dimer, and tapered towards the expected monomer mass at the tail. This again indicated dynamic equilibrium between monomer and dimer states, and that higher-order species were also present in the main peak, but at a much smaller fraction than dimers. Thus, the Bcc miniTRIM was predominantly dimeric in solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Published AUC analysis of freshly purified full-length TRIM5 did not show evidence of B-box mediated self-association, even at a loading concentration that is six-fold higher than the measured miniTRIM dimerization affinity.
source: Published AUC analysis of freshly purified full-length TRIM5 did not show evidence of B-box mediated self-association, even at a loading concentration that is six-fold higher than our measured miniTRIM dimerization affinity (Langelier et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Langelier et al., 2008.

claim: Uncoupling of the B-box from the full coiled-coil and RING domains appears to have amplified its propensity for oligomerization.
source: Uncoupling of the B-box from the full coiled-coil and RING domains therefore appears to have amplified its propensity for oligomerization.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparison of miniTRIM and full-length TRIM5α behavior.

claim: Upon incubation, full-length TRIM5α has a clear propensity to assemble into hexagonal arrays even at low μM concentrations.
source: Another difference is that, upon incubation, full-length TRIM5α has a clear propensity to assemble into hexagonal arrays – and by inference, three-way B-box/B-box interactions – even at low μM concentrations (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016; and this study).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016) and data from this study.

claim: Extended incubation of miniTRIMs did not result in lattice formation but only produced higher molecular weight aggregates.
source: Since the miniTRIMs lack an intact coiled-coil, extended incubation did not result in lattice formation but only produced higher molecular weight aggregates (not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: Artificial uncoupling of the B-box 2 domain from the full coiled-coil and RING domains has stabilized the B-box dimer form.
source: Our interpretation of all of these observations is that artificial uncoupling of the B-box 2 domain from the full coiled-coil and RING domains has stabilized the B-box dimer form.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on the experimental observations.

claim: In context of the full-length protein, assembly cooperativity drives the B-box into the trimer form.
source: In context of the full-length protein, assembly cooperativity drives the B-box into the trimer form
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparison of miniTRIM and full-length TRIM5α behavior.

claim: The B-box dimer might represent an intermediate state that can incorporate an additional B-box domain to form the trimer.
source: and so the B-box dimer might represent an intermediate state that can incorporate an additional B-box domain to form the trimer.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: The Bcc miniTRIM dimers can open slightly like a clam shell, which could lead to a wider opening and provide access to a third subunit.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, our structures indicate that the Bcc miniTRIM dimers can open slightly like a clam shell, which we imagine can lead to a wider opening and provide access to a third subunit (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The B-box trimer is what facilitates hexagonal lattice assembly, at least in vitro.
source: Nevertheless, it seems clear that the B-box trimer is what facilitates hexagonal lattice assembly, at least in vitro.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Charge reversal mutations in the top layer of interactions (E102K, K103E, E102K/K103E) diminished restriction activity.
source: Charge reversal mutations in the top layer of interactions (E102K, K103E, E102K/K103E) diminished restriction activity (Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by restriction assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ring of salt bridges in the top layer has an appreciable contribution to higher-order TRIM5α assembly.
source: confirming that this ring of salt bridges has an appreciable contribution to higher-order TRIM5α assembly.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the mutagenesis results.

claim: Individual charge reversals in the bottom layer (E120R, R121E) severely abrogated restriction activity.
source: Individual charge reversals in the bottom layer (E120R, R121E) severely abrogated restriction activity (Figure 4B)
evidence: This claim is supported by restriction assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The E120R/R121E double mutation did not have a compensatory effect on restriction activity.
source: However, the E120R/R121E double mutation did not have a compensatory effect.
evidence: This claim is based on restriction assay data.

claim: The lack of compensatory effect in the E120R/R121E double mutant is consistent with the structures since Arg121 is involved in both a salt bridge and a hydrophobic packing interaction with Trp117.
source: This is in contrast with previous studies (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009; Li and Sodroski, 2008) but is consistent with the structures since Arg121 is involved in both a salt bridge and a hydrophobic packing interaction with Trp117.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The W117E mutation abolishes restriction activity.
source: In the middle, hydrophobic layer, the W117E mutation was previously shown to abolish restriction activity (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009), which we have confirmed here (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by restriction assay data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to Diaz-Griffero et al., 2009.

claim: The W117A mutant still harbored some restriction activity, most likely because the hydrophobic layer remains stabilized by an outer ring of leucines.
source: Interestingly, however, the W117A mutant still harbored some restriction activity, most likely because the hydrophobic layer remains stabilized by an outer ring of leucines.
evidence: This claim is based on restriction assay data and structural inference.

claim: Alanine substitution mutants for Leu118 and Leu132 had measurable restriction activity, whereas aspartate substitutions were more significantly disruptive.
source: As with Trp117, alanine substitution mutants for Leu118 (Figure 4D) and Leu132 (Figure 4E) had measurable restriction activity, whereas aspartate substitutions were more significantly disruptive.
evidence: This claim is supported by restriction assay data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: L105A had full restriction activity and L106A did not restrict HIV-1.
source: Of the remaining two leucines, L105A had full activity and L106A did not restrict HIV-1 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by restriction assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The mutagenesis results are consistent with the structures since Leu105 is only partially buried, whereas Leu106 is completely buried within both the dimer and trimer interfaces.
source: These results are again consistent with the structures since Leu105 is only partially buried, whereas Leu106 is completely buried within both the dimer and trimer interfaces.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: Steady state expression levels of the TRIM5α B-box 2 domain mutants varied considerably.
source: Interestingly, we found that steady state expression levels of the TRIM5α B-box 2 domain mutants varied considerably, as noted previously (Diaz-Griffero et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G and a citation to Diaz-Griffero et al., 2007.

claim: There was an inverse correlation between the steady state expression levels of the mutant proteins and restriction activity.
source: and that furthermore there was an inverse correlation between the steady state expression levels of the mutant proteins and restriction activity (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The best expressing mutants (e.g., W117E and R121E) did not restrict HIV, whereas the lowest expressing mutant (L105A) had WT-like restriction activity.
source: The best expressing mutants (e.g., W117E and R121E) did not restrict HIV, whereas the lowest expressing mutant (L105A) had WT-like restriction activity.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of expression levels and restriction activity data.

claim: The expression levels inversely correlated with in vitro assembly efficiency.
source: The expression levels also inversely correlated with in vitro assembly efficiency – W117E and R121E did not assemble, whereas L105A assembled efficiently (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; also see below).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of expression levels and assembly data.

claim: The ability to assemble reduces steady state protein levels because TRIM5α proteins that assemble are turned over more rapidly in cells.
source: We therefore speculate that the ability to assemble reduces steady state protein levels because TRIM5α proteins that assemble are turned over more rapidly in cells.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the observed correlations.

claim: The ability of TRIM5α to assemble correlates with its ability to restrict HIV-1.
source: An extension of this argument is that the ability of TRIM5α to assemble correlates with its ability to restrict HIV-1.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed correlations between assembly, expression, and restriction.

claim: About 50% of WT TRIM5-21R was consistently found in the pellet in capsid binding assays.
source: In control experiments, about 50% of WT TRIM5-21R was consistently found in the pellet (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by capsid binding assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Essentially all of the B-box mutants tested had detectable capsid binding activity.
source: Essentially all of the B-box mutants tested had detectable capsid binding activity
evidence: This claim is based on capsid binding assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All B-box mutants contained an intact SPRY domain.
source: which was expected because all of these constructs contained an intact SPRY domain
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental design.

claim: The R121E mutation that abolished restriction still supported capsid binding in a similar assay.
source: and because the R121E mutation that abolished restriction still supported capsid binding in a similar assay (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011.

claim: Weaker or no capsid binding correlated with weaker or no restriction activity.
source: Nevertheless, our results showed that weaker or no capsid binding correlated with weaker or no restriction activity (Table 2)
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of capsid binding and restriction data summarized in Table 2.

claim: B-box 2 domain mediated interactions promote efficient capsid recognition.
source: confirming that B-box 2 domain mediated interactions promote efficient capsid recognition.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the mutagenesis and binding data.

claim: Purified TRIM5-21R assembles spontaneously into hexagonal arrays when incubated in low salt buffer at about 1 mg/mL.
source: Previously, purified TRIM5-21R was shown to assemble spontaneously into hexagonal arrays when incubated in low salt buffer at about 1 mg/mL (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011.

claim: The R121E mutant did not assemble spontaneously even at concentrations up to 30 mg/mL.
source: In contrast, the R121E mutant did not assemble spontaneously even at concentrations up to 30 mg/mL (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations that gave the most significant reductions in restriction activity (L106A, W117E, L118D, and L132D) also prevented assembly at all protein concentrations tested (up to 18 mg/mL).
source: We found that mutations that gave the most significant reductions in restriction activity (L106A, W117E, L118D, and L132D) also prevented assembly at all protein concentrations tested (up to 18 mg/mL) (Table 2 and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on assembly assay data summarized in Table 2.

claim: L118A and L132A mutations supported hexagonal lattice assembly, but only at high protein concentrations and to a more limited extent compared to WT.
source: Two of the mutations that supported intermediate restriction activity (L118A and L132A) also supported hexagonal lattice assembly, but only at high protein concentrations and to a more limited extent compared to WT (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The W117A mutant failed to assemble in standard low salt buffer at both 1 and 5 mg/mL, but at high protein concentrations and higher salt (>250 mM NaCl), it assembled into striated arrays.
source: A third intermediate mutation, W117A, altered the assembly phenotype of TRIM5-21R. This mutant failed to assemble in standard low salt buffer at both 1 and 5 mg/mL, but at high protein concentrations and higher salt (>250 mM NaCl), it assembled into striated arrays (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The L105A mutation formed macramé-like networks under the same conditions as WT (low salt buffer and 1 mg/mL protein).
source: Interestingly, the L105A mutation (full restriction activity) also altered the spontaneous assembly behavior of TRIM5-21R. Under the same conditions as WT (low salt buffer and 1 mg/mL protein), L105A formed macramé-like networks that appeared distinct from either the hexagonal or striated arrays (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The L105A mutant showed similar behavior to WT in the co-assembly assay with virtually all tubes uniformly decorated.
source: and the L105A mutant (Figure 7B) showed similar behavior in this assay; that is, virtually all the tubes were uniformly decorated, and the decorations looked similar to each other and to those made by WT TRIM5α (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7B and a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: For both WT and L105A, regions of local order with hexagonal rings having the expected dimensions for a TRIM hexamer were observed in tomograms.
source: As expected, the peripheral TRIM5α layers exhibited a high degree of disorder, but for both WT (Figure 8A) and L105A (Figure 8B), we could clearly observe regions of local order with hexagonal rings having the expected dimensions for a TRIM hexamer.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: A proportion of the L105A decorations appeared more ladder-like, but the distances between the repeating units were similar to the TRIM hexagon dimensions.
source: Interestingly, a proportion of the L105A decorations appeared more ladder-like (Figure 8C), but again the distances between the repeating units were similar to the TRIM hexagon dimensions.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Although there is no clear structural explanation for the spontaneous assembly behavior of the L105A mutant, it can form hexagonal arrays when it binds CA tubes in vitro.
source: We therefore conclude that, although there is no clear structural explanation for the spontaneous assembly behavior of the L105A mutant, it can nevertheless form hexagonal arrays when it binds CA tubes in vitro.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the assembly and tomography data.

claim: The inability of L105A to form flat lattices suggests that B-box/B-box interactions might have some link to lattice curvature.
source: The inability of this mutant to form flat lattices (the endpoints of both the spontaneous assembly and template driven methods) suggests that B-box/B-box interactions might have some link to lattice curvature.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the assembly behavior of the L105A mutant.

claim: The W117A mutant decorated CA tubes, but the decorations were more limited in extent compared to either WT or L105A, and regions of undecorated CA were more readily apparent.
source: We also used the co-assembly assay to characterize the W117A mutant that assembled into striated arrays (Figure 6D). This mutant also decorated the CA tubes, but the decorations were more limited in extent compared to either WT or L105A, and regions of undecorated CA were more readily apparent in the projection images (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The tomograms of W117A-decorated tubes revealed considerable disorder in the overlaying TRIM lattice, and hexagon-shaped decorations were not easily discerned.
source: Similarly, the tomograms revealed considerable disorder in the overlaying TRIM lattice, and hexagon-shaped decorations were not easily discerned (not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on electron tomography analysis.

claim: There is a general correlation between TRIM5α restriction activity in cells, capsid binding efficiency in vitro, and hexagonal lattice assembly in vitro.
source: In summary, our analysis of structure-based B-box 2 domain mutations support a general correlation between TRIM5α restriction activity in cells, capsid binding efficiency in vitro, and hexagonal lattice assembly in vitro.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined mutagenesis, binding, and assembly data.

claim: Both capsid recognition and antiviral restriction are facilitated by B-box mediated assembly of TRIM5α into a hexagonal lattice that wraps around the viral capsid.
source: Our results therefore fit the model wherein both capsid recognition and antiviral restriction are facilitated by B-box mediated assembly of TRIM5α into a hexagonal lattice that wraps around the viral capsid.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined experimental results.

claim: The low-resolution structure of the TRIM5α hexagonal lattice consists of large lobes of density at the two-fold and three-fold symmetric positions connected by thin linkers of density.
source: The low-resolution structure of the TRIM5α hexagonal lattice consists of large lobes of density at the two-fold and three-fold symmetric positions connected by thin linkers of density (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016).

claim: The thin linkers in the TRIM5α hexagonal lattice are made by the antiparallel coiled-coil dimer scaffold.
source: The thin linkers are made by the antiparallel coiled-coil dimer scaffold
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Goldstone et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Sanchez et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016).

claim: The two-fold lobes in the TRIM5α hexagonal lattice are made by the SPRY domain.
source: and the two-fold lobes are made by the SPRY domain (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Goldstone et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Sanchez et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Goldstone et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Sanchez et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016).

claim: The three-fold vertexes of the TRIM5α hexagonal lattice are made by B-box 2 domain trimers.
source: Our structural and biochemical analyses indicate that the three-fold vertexes are made by B-box 2 domain trimers.
evidence: This claim is based on the structural and biochemical data from this study.

claim: A molecular model of a flat TRIM5α hexagonal lattice was built by combining the miniTRIM trimer crystal structure with the B-box/coiled-coil dimer structure (PDB 4TN3).
source: By combining our miniTRIM trimer crystal structure with that of the B-box/coiled-coil dimer (PDB 4TN3) (Goldstone et al., 2014), we built a molecular model of a flat TRIM5α hexagonal lattice (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim describes the computational modeling approach.

claim: The unit cell spacing of the TRIM5α hexagonal lattice model is 338.5 Å, which is an almost exact match to the observed value for rhesus TRIM5α (340 Å).
source: The unit cell spacing of this model is 338.5 Å, which is an almost exact match to the observed value for rhesus TRIM5α (340 Å) (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the model with experimental data from Li et al., 2016.

claim: All of the SPRY domains are located on one side of the lattice plane where they could bind the capsid simultaneously.
source: All of the SPRY domains are located on one side of the lattice plane (Figure 9B, blue spheres), where they could bind the capsid simultaneously.
evidence: This claim is based on the molecular model shown in Figure 9B.

claim: At the three-fold vertexes, the N-terminal ends of the B-boxes point toward the other side of the lattice plane, suggesting that the RING domains are oriented away from the capsid.
source: At the three-fold vertexes, the N-terminal ends of the B-boxes point toward the other side of the lattice plane. This suggests that the RING domains are oriented away from the capsid (Figure 9B, red spheres).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the molecular model shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The higher-order TRIM scaffold compartmentalizes the biochemical activities of the RING and SPRY domains.
source: This molecular architecture indicates that the higher-order TRIM scaffold also compartmentalizes the biochemical activities of the RING and SPRY domains.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the molecular model.

claim: When TRIM5α binds to a retroviral capsid, it must accommodate the variable surface curvature of the capsid.
source: When TRIM5α binds to a retroviral capsid, it must accommodate the variable surface curvature of the capsid.
evidence: This claim is based on the known structural properties of retroviral capsids.

claim: Capsid lattice curvature is generated by rigid body hinge motions between subunits.
source: Capsid lattice curvature is generated by rigid body hinge motions between subunits, and we have previously identified such hinges by comparing crystallographically independent structures of the hexameric and pentameric capsid building blocks (Pornillos et al., 2009; 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Pornillos et al., 2009; 2011).

claim: Superposition of the miniTRIM structures revealed that the coiled-coil can swing relative to the B-box 2 domain.
source: As illustrated in Figure 10A, superposition of the miniTRIM structures revealed that the coiled-coil can swing relative to the B-box 2 domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Flexion occurs about the B-box/coiled-coil interface, which is lined almost exclusively by aliphatic sidechains.
source: Flexion occurs about the B-box/coiled-coil interface, which is lined almost exclusively by aliphatic sidechains (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: In context of full-length TRIM5, the B-box/coiled-coil interface is a quaternary contact between the subunits of the native dimer.
source: Note that in context of full-length TRIM5, this 'greasy' interface is a quaternary contact between the subunits of the native dimer.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structure of full-length TRIM5α.

claim: Bending of the first two turns of the coiled-coil helix in the dimer subunits produced the greatest change in orientation of the B-box relative to the coiled-coil.
source: Bending of the first two turns of the coiled-coil helix in the dimer subunits produced the greatest change in orientation of the B-box relative to the coiled-coil
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis.

claim: In context of the trimer, the three coiled-coils do not contact each other and can therefore move independently.
source: In context of the trimer, the three coiled-coils do not contact each other and can therefore move independently (Figure 10C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 10C and 10D.

claim: TRIM5α uses the same general mechanism as retroviral capsids – flexion across quaternary interfaces and local conformational variations – to generate variable lattice curvature.
source: We conclude that TRIM5α uses the same general mechanism as retroviral capsids – flexion across quaternary interfaces and local conformational variations – to generate variable lattice curvature.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparison of TRIM5α and capsid structural flexibility.

claim: B-box mediated interactions promote dimerization of the upstream RING domain and E3 ligase activity.
source: B-box mediated interactions also promote dimerization of the upstream RING domain and E3 ligase activity (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Pertel et al., 2011; Yudina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2011; Pertel et al., 2011; Yudina et al., 2015).

claim: The catalytically active RING configuration is more structurally compatible with a B-box dimer.
source: The catalytically active RING configuration is more structurally compatible with a B-box dimer
evidence: This claim is an inference based on structural considerations.

claim: It is possible that the B-box switches its oligomeric configuration to facilitate enzymatic function.
source: and it is therefore possible that the B-box switches its oligomeric configuration to facilitate enzymatic function.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: It is possible for a RING-containing subunit to act simultaneously as ligase and ubiquitination substrate within the same E2-Ub/E3 complex, as biochemically demonstrated for the RING domain of RNF4.
source: In principle, it is possible for a RING-containing subunit to act simultaneously as ligase and ubiquitination substrate within the same E2-Ub/E3 complex, as biochemically demonstrated for the RING domain of RNF4 (Plechanovová et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Plechanovová et al., 2011.

claim: Modeling studies support a mechanism by which the B-box trimer could contribute to TRIM5α self-ubiquitination.
source: Nevertheless, our modeling studies also support a mechanism by which the B-box trimer could contribute to TRIM5α self-ubiquitination.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: A B-box trimer could bring together three RINGs, with the first two acting as the E3 ligase and the third acting as the substrate.
source: Specifically, a B-box trimer could bring together three RINGs, with the first two acting as the E3 ligase and the third acting as the substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Folding of the RING/B-box linker into a 4-helix bundle restricts the RING dimer to the outer surface of the TRIM hexagonal lattice, on the opposite side of the capsid binding surface.
source: More important, our analysis further suggests that folding of the RING/B-box linker into a 4-helix bundle restricts the RING dimer to the outer surface of the TRIM hexagonal lattice, i.e., on the opposite side of the capsid binding surface.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Spatial compartmentalization of the RING domain facilitates formation of exposed polyubiquitin chains that can recruit downstream cytosolic factors to promote restriction and/or interferon signaling.
source: We suggest that this spatial compartmentalization facilitates formation of exposed polyubiquitin chains that can recruit downstream cytosolic factors to promote restriction and/or interferon signaling.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: Residues 72–82 of the L1 linker are disordered in the monomeric RING structure, but are folded into a 4-helix bundle in the dimeric RING.
source: Residues 72–82 are disordered in the monomeric RING structure, but are folded into a 4-helix bundle in the dimeric RING (Lienlaf et al., 2011; Yudina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies (Lienlaf et al., 2011; Yudina et al., 2015).

claim: A RING monomer has a longer (and presumably more flexible) linker to the B-box than a RING dimer subunit.
source: Thus, a RING monomer has a longer (and presumably more flexible) linker to the B-box than a RING dimer subunit.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structural differences between monomeric and dimeric RING.

claim: In the ensemble of models with flexibly tethered monomeric RINGs, the vast majority of the RING domains are located above the plane of the trimer.
source: In the resulting ensemble, the vast majority of the RING domains are located above the plane of the trimer (Figure 11A, right).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Even flexibly tethered monomeric RINGs are predominantly located on one side of the lattice and away from the capsid.
source: Thus, even flexibly tethered monomeric RINGs are predominantly located on one side of the lattice and away from the capsid.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: In a subset of models, the RING/B-box linker folds down, bringing the RING domain against the trimer vertex.
source: In a subset of our models, the RING/B-box linker folds down, in a configuration that brings the RING domain against the trimer vertex (Figure 11A, left).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Close packing of the RING domain and/or the RING/B-box linker against the trimer interface might explain the observation that the RING domain contributes to the efficiency of TRIM5α higher-order assembly.
source: In principle, close packing of the RING domain and/or the RING/B-box linker against the trimer interface might explain the observation that the RING domain contributes to the efficiency of TRIM5α higher-order assembly (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the modeling results and a citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Analysis of the 12-residue linker sequence (83EVKLSPEEGQKV94) using the PEP-FOLD server predicts that residues 87–94 have some propensity to fold into a short helix.
source: Analysis of this sequence using the PEP-FOLD server (Shen et al., 2014) predicts that residues 87–94 have some propensity to fold into a short helix
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction using PEP-FOLD.

claim: The dimeric RING/B-box linker might be a hinge rather than a flexible tether.
source: and we therefore speculate that the dimeric RING/B-box linker might actually be a hinge rather than a flexible tether.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the computational prediction.

claim: Since E2-Ub binding imposes additional spatial constraints, stereochemical clashes can only be avoided if the RING dimer is positioned above the B-box trimer.
source: Since E2-Ub binding imposes additional spatial constraints, stereochemical clashes can only be avoided if the RING dimer is positioned above the B-box trimer (Figure 11B).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 11B.

claim: In context of the TRIM hexagonal lattice, the B-box trimer spatially restricts the RING domain, such that an active E3 ligase can only form on the side of the lattice that faces the cytoplasm.
source: We therefore conclude that in context of the TRIM hexagonal lattice, the B-box trimer spatially restricts the RING domain, such that an active E3 ligase can only form on the side of the lattice that faces the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: A B-box dimer also restricted RING positions, but to a lesser extent than the trimer.
source: We also performed the same analysis on the B-box dimer; as expected, it also restricted RING positions, but to a lesser extent than the trimer (not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: The principal Ub attachment sites in TRIM5α are in the RING domain (Lys45 and Lys51).
source: The principal Ub attachment sites are in the RING domain (Lys45 and Lys51) (Fletcher et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fletcher et al., 2015.

claim: A B-box trimer suggests a mechanism for self-ubiquitination because it clusters three RING domains.
source: Although a B-box dimer is more naturally compatible with a RING dimer, a B-box trimer suggests an intuitively appealing mechanism for self-ubiquitination because it clusters three RING domains.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on structural considerations.

claim: In the proposed self-ubiquitination model, two of the RING domains would dimerize and orient an E2-conjugated Ub for nucleophilic attack by the third RING.
source: In this model, two of the RING domains would dimerize and orient an E2-conjugated Ub for nucleophilic attack by the third RING (Yudina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on a proposed mechanism and a citation to Yudina et al., 2015.

claim: Stereochemically acceptable conformations were identified that simultaneously allow trimerization of the B-box, dimerization of two RINGs, binding of the RING dimer to a Ub-conjugated E2, and positioning of the appropriate lysine in the third RING for nucleophilic attack of the E2-Ub thioester bond.
source: As illustrated in Figure 11C, we were able to identify stereochemically acceptable conformations that simultaneously allow trimerization of the B-box, dimerization of two RINGs, binding of the RING dimer to a Ub-conjugated E2, and positioning of the appropriate lysine in the third RING for nucleophilic attack of the E2-Ub thioester bond.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 11C.

claim: B-box trimerization is compatible with RING activation and TRIM5α self-ubiquitination.
source: Thus, although our modeling approach is somewhat crude, the results indicate that B-box trimerization is compatible with RING activation and TRIM5α self-ubiquitination.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the computational modeling results.
